title: Book 2 — Euterpe, Chapter 384
paragraphs: So when Apries, leading his foreign mercenaries, and Amasis, at the head of the whole body of the Egyptians, approached one another and came to the city of Momemphis, they joined battle. Although the foreign troops fought well, they were far outnumbered and were defeated because of this. Apries is said to have supposed that not even a god could cause him to cease from his rule, so firmly did he think it was established. In that battle, then, he was defeated, and being taken alive he was brought away to the city of Saïs, to what had formerly been his own dwelling but was henceforth the palace of Amasis. There he was kept in the palace for some time, and Amasis treated him well. But at last, since the Egyptians blamed Amasis, saying that he was not acting rightly in keeping alive a man who was the greatest enemy of both themselves and him, he handed Apries over to the Egyptians, and they strangled him; afterwards they buried him in the burial place of his fathers, which is in the temple of Athene, close to the sanctuary, on the left as you enter. The men of Saïs buried all those of this district who had been kings within the temple; for the tomb of Amasis too, though farther from the sanctuary than that of Apries and his forefathers, is also within the temple court. It consists of a colonnade of stone of great size, with pillars carved to resemble date palms and otherwise sumptuously adorned; and within the colonnade are double doors, and inside the doors a burial chamber.
